The crystal is described in a hexagonal unit cell with lattice parameters a = b = 3.1095175 Å and c = 5.055804 Å, with interaxial angles α = β = 90° and γ = 119.99998928°, essentially 120°. The cell contains four atoms total, one each of aluminum, silicon, carbon, and nitrogen, matching the declared input composition AlSiCN. The structure adopts space group number 156, P3m1, with Hall symbol P 3 -2", a trigonal polar space group with threefold rotational symmetry about the c-axis and mirror planes perpendicular to the basal plane.

All coordinates are given in fractional form relative to the lattice vectors. The input and standard crystallographic frames are related by the transformation q_standard = P q_input + s, where the matrix P is essentially the identity (diagonal elements 1.0000000000000002, with off-diagonal terms on the order of 10⁻¹⁷ or smaller) and the origin shift s is (3.3333333323189623 × 10⁻⁷, 0.9999996666666667, 0.0). This near-identity transformation with a small origin offset means the input and standard cells are practically coincident, with the shift primarily affecting the second fractional coordinate by approximately one unit (equivalent to a lattice translation).

The four atoms occupy two distinct types of Wyckoff positions, both of multiplicity one. Aluminum and carbon share the 1b site at in-plane fractional coordinates (1/3, 2/3), stacked along the c-axis at different heights: aluminum sits at z = 0.507161, while carbon is at z = 0.108605. Silicon and nitrogen occupy the 1c site at (2/3, 1/3), with silicon at z = 0.99731 (very close to the top face of the cell) and nitrogen at z = 0.636924. Thus the structure consists of two vertical columns of atoms: one column at the (1/3, 2/3) position containing carbon near the base and aluminum near the middle, and a second column at (2/3, 1/3) containing nitrogen in the upper-middle region and silicon near the top. The threefold symmetry and mirror planes of P3m1 relate these positions across the cell.

The positional values were rounded to six decimal places in the input. Two small corrections are required to recover the exact geometry. The silicon atom, initially given at (0.666666, 0.333334, 0.99731), must be displaced by (+1.0000000000287557 × 10⁻⁶, −1.0000000000287557 × 10⁻⁶, 0.0), bringing its in-plane coordinates to exactly (2/3, 1/3). Similarly, the nitrogen atom at (0.666666, 0.333334, 0.636924) requires the same in-plane correction of (+10⁻⁶, −10⁻⁶, 0.0) to reach the ideal (2/3, 1/3) position. These adjustments reflect rounding in the input rather than true deviations from the symmetry sites, and they preserve the real geometry implied by the space-group assignment.
